stories.title: The South Florida Real Estate Market Leans Evermore on the Wealthy
stories.excerpt: The South Florida market remains strong as wealthy Northerners continue to relocate down south, even as the rest of the country faces headwinds due to rising interest rates, speakers agreed at Commercial Observer’s South Florida Capital & Development Forum, held Oct. 15 at Don Peebles’ Bath Club in Miami Beach. “Were selling unaffordable apartments,” said Gil Dezer, president of Dezer Development, who’s building the Bentley condo tower in Sunny Isles Beach, at a panel hosted by Zachary G. Darrow, chairman and CEO of DarrowEverett. “There’s a new billionaire minted in San Francisco every week, and they want to be in Miami,” added Genghis Hadi, co-founder and managing principal of Nahla Capital, which is redeveloping Miami Beach’s oceanfront Raleigh hotel, its first project in South Florida. Isaac Toledano of BH Group, who’s developing a skyscraper nearby, agreed: “When we went out to market the financing, we got multiple term sheets, so I think it’s still very encouraging.” Panelists speak at Commercial Observer’s South Florida Capital & Development Forum. The buyer pool is changing, said Christine Martinez de Castro, chief sales and marketing officer CMC Group, which is developing the Four Seasons condo in Coconut Grove. Domestic buyers have remained strong presences, while Europeans are starting to overtake Latin Americans. bullets: Wealthy migrants from North and West drive South Florida luxury condo demand; Gil Dezer, Genghis Hadi report strong sales.
New financing available despite national headwinds; multiple term sheets received for Miami projects.
Miami capturing high-net-worth inflow while rest of country faces rate headwinds.
stories.summary: South Florida's luxury residential market remains insulated from national rate pressures, driven by persistent wealthy relocation from Northern and West Coast metros. Developers report strong financing availability and robust demand for high-end condos, with new projects in Miami Beach and Sunny Isles attracting multiple term sheets. The market is effectively bifurcated: luxury segment thriving on migration flows while broader U.S. multifamily faces affordability and refinance stress.
stories.impact: Signals a divergence in South Florida's multifamily ecosystem: ultra-luxury condo development remains well-capitalized and demand-constrained, but this wealth concentration may crowd out workforce and market-rate multifamily supply and investment. Developers should evaluate whether South Florida multifamily opportunities outside luxury high-rise exist or whether capital is chasing condo conversions and new construction that compete with rental product for land and entitlements in core Miami/Miami Beach.

stories.title: Amazon Leases 91K-SF Warehouse in Everett
stories.excerpt: Amazon has leased a 90,970-square-foot warehouse in Everett for the company’s Leo satellite division. Two years after vacating a warehouse in Everett, Amazon⁠.com Inc. (Nasdaq: AMZN⁠) has returned to the building with a new lease, and the Seattle-based tech giant will occupy the industrial facility at 6611 Associated Blvd., reported the Puget Sound Business Journal. Amazon had occupied the industrial facility from at least 2018 until 2024, when it let the lease expire. The property hasn’t been physically occupied since at least 2022, and Colliers began marketing the property for lease in March of 2024. Located nearby is the 167,000-square-foot logistics hub for Amazon’s orbital satellite division, which was repurposed from a former delivery station. Amazon Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper, is the company’s low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite broadband network. The subsidiary was established in 2019 to deploy a large satellite Internet constellation providing low-latency connectivity. The post Amazon Leases 91K-SF Warehouse in Everett appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Amazon Leo (satellite division) leases 91K SF warehouse in Everett, WA; returns after 2-year vacancy.
Company now operates dual Everett facilities: 91K SF + 167K SF repurposed logistics hub for orbital satellites.
Amazon expanding fixed infrastructure for broadband constellation project in Seattle metro.
stories.summary: Amazon has leased a 90,970-square-foot warehouse in Everett, Washington for its Leo satellite broadband division, marking the company's return to a facility it vacated in 2022. This lease complements a nearby 167,000-square-foot repurposed logistics hub also dedicated to Project Kuiper (Leo). The dual-facility setup signals material operational expansion in the Puget Sound region for Amazon's satellite internet infrastructure.
stories.impact: Amazon's satellite infrastructure build-out in Everett represents a new class of anchor tenant demand for industrial real estate in Seattle metro and signals potential workforce in-migration (engineering, operations, manufacturing support). This could underpin multifamily demand in Snohomish County and nearby Seattle submarkets if satellite operations scale. Monitor for related supplier/contractor activity and potential supply-chain clustering around Everett logistics hub—could create secondary wave of employment-driven rental demand.

stories.title: Hanley Investment Group Arranges Sale of Milwaukee Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: Hanley Investment Group Real Estate Advisors arranged the sale of Cornerstone Shopping Center, a 13,308‑square‑foot retail center located in the North Shore trade area across from Bayshore, one of Wisconsin’s mixed‑use destinations. Hanley Investment Group’s Executive Vice President and Partner Jeff Lefko and Executive Vice President Bill Asher, in association with ParaSell, Inc., represented the seller, a private investor from North San Diego County, California. The buyer, SW Neighborhood Centers IV, an affiliate of Alabama-based commercial real estate firm Shannon Waltchack, represented itself. “We generated multiple competitive offers from private equity and institutional buyers within the first few weeks of marketing and secured an all‑cash institutional buyer that closed escrow in 45 days,” Lefko said. The property consists of two retail buildings totaling 13,308 square feet on 1.05 acres. It is located at 635‑695 West Silver Spring Drive and 5575‑5595 North Port Washington Road in Glendale, Wisconsin, and was 100% occupied at the time of the sale. The post Hanley Investment Group Arranges Sale of Milwaukee Shopping Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hanley Investment Group sold 13.3K SF retail center in Glendale, WI to Alabama-based Shannon Waltchack affiliate.
100% occupied at sale; closed in 45 days with all-cash institutional buyer after competitive marketing.
North Shore Milwaukee location across from Bayshore mixed-use development.
stories.summary: Cornerstone Shopping Center, a 13,308-square-foot fully-leased retail property in Glendale, Wisconsin (North Shore Milwaukee), sold for an undisclosed price to an affiliate of Alabama-based commercial real estate firm Shannon Waltchack. The transaction closed in 45 days with an all-cash buyer after generating multiple competitive offers in early marketing.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Story indicates institutional buyer appetite for grocery-adjacent stabilized retail in suburban Milwaukee, but does not signal demand or supply pressures affecting apartment markets. No apparent chain of effects on rents, population migration, or labor demand in the Milwaukee metro.

stories.title: Skanska Wins Excellence in Construction Award for Work on George Mason University Project
stories.excerpt: Skanska was named the recipient of a 2026 Excellence in Construction Award by the Metro Washington and Virginia Chapters of Associated Builders and Contractors for the firm’s work on George Mason University’s (GMU) Life Sciences and Engineering Building. Located on GMU’s Prince William County Science and Technology (SciTech) Campus, the $85.4 million building spans 132,000 square feet of purpose-built space. Completed in January 2025, the state-of-the-art facility features advanced research laboratories, specialized teaching facilities, and flexible innovation zones designed for breakthrough work in bioengineering, bioinformatics, and computational life sciences. The Excellence in Construction Awards annually recognize outstanding projects built by Washington-area ABC members. “This achievement highlights our continued commitment to delivering exceptional facilities and community-focused development to support higher education institutions,” said Mark Balling, executive vice president and general manager responsible for Skanska’s Mid-Atlantic region. Skanska currently has more than $1 billion in projects in progress across its Mid-Atlantic region. The post Skanska Wins Excellence in Construction Award for Work on George Mason University Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Skanska completed $85.4M, 132K SF Life Sciences & Engineering Building at GMU SciTech Campus, Prince William County.
Project finished January 2025; Skanska has $1B+ Mid-Atlantic project pipeline.
Purpose-built research and innovation facility for bioengineering, bioinformatics, life sciences.
stories.summary: Skanska completed an $85.4 million, 132,000-square-foot Life Sciences and Engineering Building at George Mason University's Prince William County Science and Technology Campus in January 2025. The facility includes advanced research labs, teaching spaces, and innovation zones. Skanska currently manages over $1 billion in active Mid-Atlantic projects.
stories.impact: GMU's SciTech Campus expansion in Prince William County signals institutional higher-ed/research anchor growth in the Northern Virginia corridor. Large capital spending on STEM facilities often precedes regional talent recruitment, startup ecosystem development, and associated workforce in-migration. Multifamily developers should monitor for follow-on demand from research staff, graduate students, and spinout company hiring in Prince William/Fairfax County submarkets. GMU's capital commitments suggest growth trajectory for the outer NoVA employment base.

stories.title: A Third of Maturing Multifamily Debt Needs Cash Infusion to Refinance
stories.excerpt: After September’s rate hike, $6.8 billion of fresh equity stands between maturing multifamily loans and a refinance. Loans written at 2021 and 2022’s low coupons are the hardest hit. 20 Exchange Place, a 54-story, 767-unit apartment tower near Wall Street that was built in 1929, was 94 percent occupied in the second quarter, and its loan is current. But the $246 million Freddie Mac loan behind it carries a 4.01 percent coupon and matures in February 2027. The property’s 2025 net operating income of $15.5 million would support a new loan of about $183 million at today’s agency rates, leaving a gap of roughly $63 million. The borrower has been calling capital from investors as needed to cover operating shortfalls, according to servicer commentary. That arithmetic is now common. CRED iQ resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028, $136 billion in all, at current new-issue coupons plus September’s rate hike. Nearly one in four (23 percent) of those loans, and 31 percent of the balance, could not refinance without new equity. Borrowers would need to bring $6.8 billion to the table. The median shortfall is 15 percent of the loan, or about $25,000 per apartment. What the hike did The Secured Overnight Financing Rate jumped from 3.62 percent to 3.85 percent on Sept. 17. Passed through to permanent loan coupons, the hike pushed 178 more loans ($4 billion of balance) below a 1.25 times coverage test and added $846 million to the equity gap. Each further 25 basis points adds roughly $1 billion more. Two more hikes would leave 39 percent of maturing multifamily debt short of a refinance. The gap is concentrated in loans written at the bottom of the rate cycle. Loans originated in 2021 and 2022, with a median coupon of 3.35 percent, now face refinancing rates roughly 2 to 3 percentage points higher. bullets: $136B multifamily debt maturing Oct 2026–Dec 2028; 31% of balance ($6.8B) requires new equity to refinance.
Loans at 2021–2022 low coupons (4.01%) cannot sustain new issuance at current rates; gap widens at agency rates.
Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae deals show 23% of loan count, 31% of balance facing refinance shortfall.
stories.summary: Nearly one-third of the $136 billion in multifamily debt maturing between October 2026 and December 2028 will require fresh equity injections to refinance at current agency rates, according to CRED iQ analysis. Loans originated in 2021–2022 at sub-4% coupons face the largest gaps; example: a $246 million Freddie Mac loan at 4.01% on Wall Street apartment tower would support only $183 million of new financing, leaving a $63 million shortfall. Borrowers are already calling capital from investors to cover deficits.
stories.impact: This is a critical signal of refinance distress cascading through the multifamily capital stack in 2026–2028. Developers should expect: (1) forced asset sales and portfolio liquidations creating acquisition opportunities at lower entry prices in some markets; (2) reduced new development starts as capital is trapped in legacy debt workouts; (3) potential yield compression in stabilized assets as distressed sellers flood the market; (4) widened spread between A+ stabilized assets and value-add/development plays. Underwriting and financing availability will tighten materially. Track maturing loans in target markets to identify potential deals and assess competitive supply impact.

stories.title: SL Green, Mori Trust Secure $2B Refi of Midtown Office Tower
stories.excerpt: SL Green Realty Corp. and a U.S. affiliate of Mori Trust Co. have secured a $2 billion refinancing of 245 Park Ave., a 44-story office tower spanning the entire block between East 46th and East 47th in Midtown Manhattan. The five-year, fixed-rate financing carries an interest rate of 6.52% and replaces the property’s previous $1.768 billion of mortgage and mezzanine financing, SL Green announced. The single-asset, single-borrower CMBS execution was arranged by a group of institutions led by JPMorgan Chase Bank. SL Green, the largest office landlord in New York City, acquired the 1.8 million-square foot property out of bankruptcy in 2022 and embarked on a robust repositioning effort with architecture firm Kohn Pedersen Fox that is expected to wrap up in the first quarter of 2027. The company sold a 49.9% interest in 245 Park Ave. to Mori Trust in June 2022. Completed in 1967, the tower sits across from Grand Central Terminal and is currently 100% leased to tenants including Société Générale, Ares Management, Houlihan Lokey, Carlyle and EQT Partners. “This transaction brings our $7.0 billion 2026 financing plan to near completion, generating incremental liquidity, strengthening our balance sheet and extending our debt maturities,” said Harrison Sitomer, President and Chief Investment Officer of SL Green in a statement. The post SL Green, Mori Trust Secure $2B Refi of Midtown Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SL Green and Mori Trust refi 245 Park Ave. Midtown Manhattan for $2B at 6.52% fixed, 5-year term.
Replaces $1.768B prior debt; single-asset CMBS execution led by JPMorgan Chase.
SL Green repositioning 1.8M SF office tower; completion expected Q1 2027; 100% leased to institutional tenants.
stories.summary: SL Green Realty Corp. and Mori Trust Co. secured a $2 billion refinancing of 245 Park Avenue, a 1.8 million-square-foot office tower in Midtown Manhattan, at a 6.52% fixed rate over five years. The single-asset CMBS transaction replaces $1.768 billion of prior financing and was structured by JPMorgan Chase Bank. SL Green is mid-repositioning effort expected to complete in Q1 2027; the tower is currently 100% leased to institutional tenants including Société Générale and Ares Management.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, the successful CMBS execution signals market capacity for trophy office assets and institutional capital appetite for marquee New York City real estate undergoing value-add repositioning. Note that office-to-residential conversion is not mentioned; this suggests office repositioning (rather than adaptive reuse) remains the capital path for elite Manhattan towers. Multifamily developers should monitor office market stabilization and any relaxation of office-to-residential restrictions in Manhattan that might unlock conversion opportunities in secondary class B/C office.

stories.title: Stimdel Properties Files Plans to Build 612 Apartments in Astoria
stories.excerpt: Stimdel Properties, an affiliate of Uruguay-based investment firm HC Corporation, has filed plans to bring 612 new apartments to 12-12 33rd Avenue in Astoria, Queens, according to a rezoning application filed with New York City’s Department of City Planning last week. The plans, filed by Stimdel, call for the construction of five mixed-use buildings, ranging from five to nine stories tall, with a total of 50,000 square feet of commercial and manufacturing space. A portion of the 612 units will be designated as affordable housing, according to the project description. The site, located between 12th and 13th streets along 33rd Avenue in Queens, is currently home to several one-story industrial and office buildings. The landmarked Barkin, Levin & Company Office Pavilion building adjacent to the development site would also be “retained” as part of the project, according to the filing. “The development site currently represents a nonconforming industrial use at the border of a residential area of Astoria,” Stimdel wrote in its filing. “The rezoning would allow redevelopment of this underutilized block for a mix of uses, including local retail, community facility space and a substantial number of affordable housing units, that will blend with surrounding residential and community facility uses to create a cohesive neighborhood.” The project description doesn’t include any information about proposed amenities for the residents. The application still needs to go through several steps ahead of approval, including a review by the City Planning Commission, a community board review and a review by the borough president. News of the filing comes after a pair of Queens-based developers — Dominick Acquista and Lorenzo Devardo — submitted plans last month to replace three industrial buildings at 31-29 Vernon Boulevard in Astoria with a new 20-story residential tower, as Commercial Observer reported at the time. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Stimdel Properties (HC Corporation affiliate) files plans for 612 apartments in Astoria, Queens at 12-12 33rd Avenue.
Five mixed-use buildings (5–9 stories), 50K SF commercial/manufacturing, partial affordable housing component.
Rezoning of industrial-to-residential site at border of Astoria residential area; landmark building retained.
stories.summary: Stimdel Properties, an affiliate of Uruguay-based HC Corporation, has filed a rezoning application with New York City Department of City Planning for a 612-unit mixed-use apartment development at 12-12 33rd Avenue in Astoria, Queens. The project includes five buildings ranging from five to nine stories, 50,000 square feet of commercial and manufacturing space, and a portion of units designated as affordable housing. The site currently contains industrial and office buildings and borders a residential area.
stories.impact: Stimdel's Astoria project represents new multifamily supply entering Queens market with both market-rate and affordable components. The rezoning from industrial-to-residential use in an urban infill location signals demand-driven development in Queens outer-borough submarkets. Developers should track: (1) rezoning approval timeline and political pushback (industrial-use displacement, affordability ratios); (2) construction cost and financing feasibility given 612-unit scale and affordable mix; (3) competitive pipeline impact on Astoria rents and absorption once delivery begins (likely 2027–2029). This is representative of Queens intensification trend and suggests land supply tightening for industrial uses in NYC.

stories.title: Southern California Retail Markets Tighten as Tenant Demand Picks Up
stories.excerpt: Southern California’s retail real estate market continued to tighten in the third quarter of 2026, with positive net absorption and declining vacancy across much of the region, according to a new report released Monday from Colliers. Retail tenants absorbed about 757,600 square feet during the quarter across Los Angeles and Orange counties and the Inland Empire. Overall vacancy fell 12 basis points from the second quarter to 6.15 percent, while leasing activity totaled 2.5 million square feet. Average asking rents increased 1 cent from the previous quarter to $2.40 per square foot per month on a triple-net basis, and up 1.33 percent compared to last year. The Inland Empire led the region with 527,000 square feet of positive net absorption, bringing its year-to-date total to more than 1 million square feet. The market accounted for nearly 70 percent of the region’s third-quarter absorption, despite a 34 percent quarterly decline in leasing activity to 767,000 square feet. Vacancy in the Inland Empire fell 30 basis points to 6.9 percent, while asking rents bumped up to $1.88 per square foot. Community and neighborhood shopping centers drove demand, accounting for approximately 276,000 square feet of positive absorption and 476,000 square feet of leasing activity. Orange County recorded another strong quarter, with 180,000 square feet of positive absorption and 444,000 square feet of leasing activity. Vacancy declined 25 basis points to 3.55 percent, a five-year low, while average asking rents jumped 3 percent quarter-over-quarter to $2.65 per square foot. Power centers accounted for approximately 143,000 square feet of Orange County’s absorption, helping offset losses at lifestyle and theme-festival centers, which gave back 118,000 square feet. Meanwhile, Los Angeles County experienced more modest strength. bullets: Southern California retail (LA, Orange, Inland Empire) absorbed 757.6K SF in Q3 2026; vacancy fell to 6.15%.
Inland Empire led region with 527K SF absorption (70% of total); year-to-date absorption exceeds 1M SF.
Asking rents up $0.01/SF/month to $2.40 NNN; up 1.33% year-over-year.
stories.summary: Southern California's retail market tightened materially in Q3 2026, with positive net absorption of 757,600 square feet and vacancy declining 12 basis points to 6.15% across Los Angeles, Orange, and Inland Empire counties. The Inland Empire dominated absorption with 527,000 square feet (70% of regional total), bringing year-to-date absorption to over 1 million square feet. Asking rents increased modestly to $2.40 per square foot per month NNN, up 1.33% annually.
stories.impact: Tightening retail conditions in Inland Empire and Southern California suggest sustained tenant demand and potential rent growth—signaling economic resilience in the region. However, this is secondary to multifamily development outlook. The retail tightness indicates competitive land use pressure and may limit industrial-to-multifamily conversion opportunities in Inland Empire and LA County. Developers should assess whether retail demand is pulling land away from multifamily sites or whether strong retail absorption signals broader economic health supporting apartment demand. Monitor Inland Empire specifically: if retail and industrial logistics demand remain robust, land costs and availability for multifamily may tighten, raising development feasibility hurdles.

stories.title: Newly Constructed Palmdale McDonald’s Trades in All-Cash Deal
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the investment sale of a newly constructed McDonald’s property totaling approximately 4,336 square feet located at 3854 Rancho Vista Blvd in Palmdale. The current tenant will remain in operation through the sale. FSD Rancho Vista sold the property to S&R Apt. 18th Street LLC for $3.5 million. The Cushman & Wakefield team of vice chair Chris Hollenbeck and director Shane Carter represented the seller. “This sale demonstrates the continued demand for high-quality, net-leased retail assets in the Greater Los Angeles region,” said Hollenbeck. “The property’s absolute NNN ground lease, strong corporate guaranty, and brand-new construction made it an attractive investment opportunity. The all-cash, quick-close nature of this transaction—approximately one month from opening escrow—underscores both the desirability of the asset and the efficiency of the process.” The property features 2026 construction on a one-acre site. The post Newly Constructed Palmdale McDonald’s Trades in All-Cash Deal appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Newly constructed McDonald's in Palmdale, CA (4,336 SF) sold for $3.5M all-cash in ~1 month.
FSD Rancho Vista to S&R Apt. 18th Street LLC; absolute NNN ground lease with corporate guaranty.
Cushman & Wakefield transaction highlights investor appetite for net-leased QSR retail in Greater LA.
stories.summary: A newly constructed McDonald's property totaling 4,336 square feet at 3854 Rancho Vista Boulevard in Palmdale sold for $3.5 million in an all-cash transaction that closed in approximately one month. The buyer, S&R Apt. 18th Street LLC, acquired the property with an absolute triple-net ground lease and strong McDonald's corporate guaranty. Cushman & Wakefield's transaction team noted strong institutional appetite for high-quality, net-leased retail assets in Greater Los Angeles.
stories.impact: Limited multifamily relevance. Net-leased QSR properties are institutional investor staples but do not directly signal apartment demand or supply dynamics in Palmdale or Greater LA. Quick close and all-cash execution suggest investor confidence in corporate-guaranteed retail, not multifamily market fundamentals. No apparent chain of effects on apartment markets.

stories.title: Invesco Sells Publix-Anchored Property for $90M After Nearly 35 Years
stories.excerpt: Invesco has unloaded a Publix-anchored shopping center in Boca Raton, Fla., for $90.3 million, after nearly 35 years of ownership, property records show. Urban Edge Properties purchased the asset called Woodfield Plaza, a 142,893-square-foot property at 3003 West Yamato Road, near the intersection with Jog Road and about a mile from Woodfield Country Club. Along with the 42,112-square-foot Publix grocery store, tenants include Walgreens, Toojay’s, Dunkin’, Chase, Vinny’s Cafe and 16 Handles. The sale excludes a Chevron gas station and two retail bank buildings: one spanning 5,346 square feet leased to Citibank and another one spanning 3,398 square feet leased to Wells Fargo. Dallas-based Invesco purchased the 14.6-acre retail center for $20.6 million in 1993, a year after it was completed, according to records. The purchase appears to be the first acquisition in South Florida for Urban Edge, a New York-based company whose portfolio is mostly confined to the Northeast. Demand for grocery-anchored real estate has surged in recent years as the pandemic has subsided, thanks to its steady rental income and consumer base. In July, Kimco Realty dropped $109 million to buy two centers in Broward County. Publix itself has also been on a shopping spree. Since 2022, it has spent hundreds of millions to buy properties it anchors, and now owns more than 38 percent of its stores. Just this month, the Lakeland-based company paid $83.3 million for a 204,740-square-foot plaza in Miami. Representatives for Invesco and Urban Edge did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Invesco sold Woodfield Plaza (Publix-anchored) in Boca Raton to Urban Edge Properties for $90.3M after 35 years.
142.9K SF property with Publix (42.1K SF), Walgreens, Dunkin', other tenants; 14.6 acres.
Urban Edge's first South Florida acquisition; Dallas-based Invesco originally purchased center for $20.6M in 1993.
stories.summary: Invesco has divested Woodfield Plaza, a 142,893-square-foot Publix-anchored shopping center in Boca Raton, Florida, to New York-based Urban Edge Properties for $90.3 million after nearly 35 years of ownership. The property spans 14.6 acres and includes a 42,112-square-foot Publix anchor, Walgreens, Dunkin', and other retail tenants. Invesco originally acquired the center for $20.6 million in 1993; the sale represents Urban Edge's first South Florida investment.
stories.impact: Institutional investor appetite for grocery-anchored retail in South Florida remains strong, but this signals portfolio rotation and potential capital redeployment, not multifamily supply or demand pressure. However, note: Urban Edge's entry into South Florida via grocery retail suggests broader institutional investor confidence in South Florida demographics and consumer spending. Multifamily developers should monitor for follow-on investment activity by Urban Edge or similar institutional players in South Florida apartment markets, particularly workforce/market-rate segments outside luxury condo focus. Grocery-anchored retail stability may indicate underlying population and retail sales health supporting multifamily fundamentals in South Florida submarkets.
